nameStory: The guppy gets its common name from Robert John Lechmere Guppy, a Trinidad naturalist who sent specimens to the British Museum in the 1860s. It's also called the "millionfish" because of how incredibly prolific it is at reproducing, and "rainbow fish" for the dazzling array of colors males can display.
description: The guppy is a small, colorful tropical fish that's native to South America but has spread around the world. Males are tiny and flashy with elaborate fins and bright colors, while females are larger, plainer, and more silvery-brown. They're livebearers, meaning they give birth to swimming babies instead of laying eggs. Most guppies you'll encounter in New England are escaped or released aquarium fish.

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Males are thumbnail-sized at about 1 inch, while females can reach 2 inches - both much smaller than most native New England fish

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Males display brilliant patches of orange, blue, green, or red that seem to shimmer like tiny jewels, while females are mostly silvery-gray with a subtle iridescent sheen

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Males have oversized, fan-like tail fins and tall dorsal fins that may be spotted or streaked with color, feeling delicate like tissue paper when handled

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Torpedo-shaped body that's compressed from side to side, with females noticeably rounder and fuller-bodied than the slender males

idTips.label: Mouth
idTips.description: Small, upward-angled mouth positioned at the front tip of the head, perfectly sized for picking at tiny food particles at the water surface

habitat: In New England, guppies are extremely rare and only found in heated water discharge areas from power plants or other warm-water sources, as they cannot survive our cold winters. Any sightings would likely be in warm springs or artificially heated ponds and streams. They prefer shallow, slow-moving water with plenty of vegetation.

seasonality.spring: Not naturally occurring in New England's cold spring waters. Any guppies would need artificially heated water to survive.
seasonality.summer: Most likely time to spot escaped aquarium guppies in warm, shallow areas, though they won't survive the approaching winter.
seasonality.fall: Any guppies present will quickly perish as water temperatures drop below their survival threshold.
seasonality.winter: Cannot survive New England's freezing winter conditions and will be absent from all natural waters.

funFact: Female guppies can store sperm for months and produce up to eight broods of babies from a single mating, which is why they earned the nickname "millionfish" - one pregnant female can theoretically produce thousands of offspring!
confusionNotes: With only one recorded sighting in New England, guppies are unlikely to be confused with anything else due to their tiny size and brilliant male coloration. If you think you see a guppy, you're probably looking at an escaped pet fish that won't survive long in our climate.
contextualKnowledge: While guppies are beloved aquarium fish worldwide, they're considered invasive species in many warm climates where released pets have established wild populations. In New England, our cold winters act as a natural barrier preventing them from becoming established, which is actually beneficial for protecting our native fish communities.
compareHints: Since guppies are the only Poecilia species recorded in New England, compare them to other small, colorful fish like juvenile sunfish or darters. However, guppies are much smaller, have the distinctive upturned mouth, and males display far more intense, jewel-like colors than any native species. Their tropical appearance makes them unmistakable if you know what to look for.
